posts.text:
In Japan, a Kurdish man arrived from Turkey with his family through visa-free entry and settled in Kawaguchi.

As soon as he arrived in Japan, he applied for asylum. Filing an asylum application automatically halted deportation, and he took advantage of this system to continue living in Japan.

But over time, his behavior became increasingly unruly. On one occasion, more than 100 Kurds gathered at his material yard and started playing loud music. The noise became so excessive that police had to show up.

He threatened a city council member, saying, “The Japanese don't understand us now, but in 10 years, they will.”

He had come to Japan seeking asylum, yet he started intimidating the very people of the country that had taken him in.

He was later arrested on suspicion of beating and injuring a woman who was living with him.

Meanwhile, a new immigration law had come into effect in Japan.

When immigration authorities took him into custody, he told his associates, “Throw bombs at the Immigration Bureau” and “Honk your horns.”

He had applied for asylum in Japan a total of six times. His first five applications had been rejected, while his sixth application was still pending.

He had challenged the denial of asylum all the way to Japan’s Supreme Court, but lost there as well. Despite this, he continued living in Japan under provisional release.

Under the new law and the “Zero Illegal Stay Plan,” deportation proceedings moved forward.

Eventually, he was forcibly deported to Turkey from Narita Airport. As he was being put on the plane, he resisted and, while crying, told immigration officers, “I’ll get a passport and return to Japan through a neighboring country.”

Later, when a Japanese journalist visited his village in Turkey, he said over the phone, “I’ve called in the military. They’re looking for you.”

His story became an example of the abuse of Japan’s asylum system.

NIGERIANS, GO AND VERIFY (6)

SECURING LIVES AND PROPERTY: PARTNERSHIP WITH SECURITY AGENCIES

Peter Obi

In the preceding instalments, I explained how we approached governance under the Anambra Integrated Development Strategy (ANIDS), beginning with strengthening state institutions and investing in education and other critical sectors. Our conviction was that development must rest on strong institutions, capable human beings, and a secure environment.

No meaningful development can take place where lives and property are constantly under threat. Education, commerce, investment, and other productive activities can only flourish when people feel safe. This informed our approach to security. We understood that the responsibility of protecting lives and property could not be discharged through speeches and declarations alone. It required deliberate investment, effective coordination, and sustained partnership with the security agencies.

When we assumed office, Anambra faced serious security challenges. Armed robbery, bank attacks, kidnapping, and other violent criminal activities had created an atmosphere of fear. In 2006, I personally approached the then Inspector-General of Police, Mr Sunday Gabriel Ehindero, to seek urgent intervention. Following our appeal, the police authorities constituted a special team comprising experienced officers, including the late Haruna John, Alhaji Amusa Bello, and others, to confront the security challenges in the state.

We therefore made security a major priority of our administration, recognising that government must provide both the leadership and the resources required to enable security agencies to perform their duties.

EQUIPPING THE SECURITY AGENCIES

We believed that those entrusted with protecting our people must be adequately equipped. Accordingly, our administration, using funds from the security votes, provided over 600 patrol vehicles to various security agencies, including the Police, Army, Civil Defence, Customs, Immigration, NDLEA, Road Safety, Prisons, SSS, Navy, and community vigilante organisations.

Our support went beyond vehicles. We provided Armoured Personnel Carriers (APCs), armoured Hilux patrol vans, communication gadgets, repeater and linker stations, base stations, mobile vehicular radios, walkie-talkies, generators, and other logistical requirements. We also used the same security votes to provide financial support for their operations, including fuel, weekly allowances, and other essential needs of security personnel.

We paid particular attention to community security because we understood that effective policing must have a strong local presence. Again, using funds from the security votes, we provided billions of naira to the 177 communities in Anambra State to strengthen security in their respective areas. We directed traditional rulers and town union presidents to establish vigilante groups under police supervision, with the police providing uniforms for proper identification. We also contributed towards the payment of their salaries.

Additionally, we provided 250 patrol vehicles to communities across Anambra State. These vehicles were manufactured by Innoson Vehicle Manufacturing Company in Nnewi. Some towns received more than one, depending on their size and security needs. This initiative was also extended to universities and other large institutions in the state.

We also recognised that markets were particularly vulnerable because of the volume of commercial activities and the large number of people who visited them daily. Thus, in March 2014, we presented security vehicles to major markets in Onitsha and its environs. The beneficiaries included Bridge Head Market, Ogboefere Market, Building Materials Market, Ogidi, Onitsha Main Market, Marine Modern Market, Ogbaru Main Market, Ose Okwodu Market, Electronics Market, and the Amalgamated Market Traders Association.
